newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen independence in Russia's interests -Udugov.
newsitem.headline: Chechen independence in Russia's interests -Udugov.

text.p: A senior Chechen official said on Wednesday that independence for his breakaway region was in Russia's own interests and that he expected Chechnya's leader Aslan Maskhadov to meet President Boris Yeltsin this month.

"A stable and independent Chechnya may become Russia's most reliable partner in the Caucasus, able to look after the interests of both sides in the region," First Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov told Interfax news agency.
Udugov was speaking on the first anniversary of an assault by separatist fighters on the Chechen capital Grozny that helped accelerate the end of a bloody 21-month war with Russian troops.
But nearly a year after Moscow and the separatists signed a peace pact, talks between the two sides on full normalisation of relations remain stalled over the issue of Chechnya's status.

The peace agreement set aside the status question for five years. The Kremlin wants Chechnya to stay within the Russian Federation but the Chechen leadership insists that the region is already an independent entity.
Udugov said Maskhadov would probably meet Yeltsin in Moscow in mid-August to try and break the deadlock.

Hundreds of camouflage-clad veterans, some of them armed, gathered in the centre of Grozny on Wednesday to celebrate last year's assault, which led to two weeks of fierce fighting and the eventual withdrawal of Russian troops.
Late on Tuesday, Maskhadov reiterated in a televised address to his people that he wanted a comprehensive treaty with Russia that would grant Chechnya wide formal powers.
He also promised to disband all parties and movements which did not support the cause of Chechnya's independence.
Maskhadov said Chechnya should use Chechen as its official language and have its own passports and car registration plates.

Yeltsin, who said last week he wanted to meet Maskhadov, has made clear he will not discuss any deals which would give Chechnya a status different to that of other parts of the vast multi-ethnic Russian Federation.

Chechen officials have been in Moscow this week, working out details of the planned meeting between Yeltsin and Maskhadov and seeking ways to implement the Kremlin's earlier promise to provide funds to help restore Chechnya's devastated economy.
The officials have put total war damages incurred by Chechnya at 1,500 trillion roubles ($258 billion).
